prospect.name: Michael L
prospect.location: United States (time zone roughly 8-10 hours behind Bulgaria; not stated more precisely)
prospect.occupation: Works from home at a desk, in meetings all day, roughly 7 a.m. to 5-6 p.m.; specific role never asked or stated
prospect.family_status: Married, no children yet ('if we decide to have kids'); one dog; travels twice a year with his wife
prospect.training_background: New to training. Some inconsistent bodyweight and mobility work at home, nothing that stuck. Averages 3,000-4,000 steps a day. No gym experience and does not know what to do in one. No kettlebell experience.
prospect.medical: No diagnosed conditions disclosed and none asked about. Reports persistent general stiffness and pain in the low back, shoulders and hips, self-rated 4-5 out of 10 and constantly present, built up over years of desk work. Tells his wife 'my back is killing me' multiple times a week. No clinician, diagnosis, imaging or treatment mentioned at any point.

signals: Wants a former self back and says so in the first thirty seconds: 'my body's just really stiff, and it's not like how it felt when I was in my 20s.'
Lost ground to a specific hard season — a desk job that escalated: 'it just has been like a slow buildup of work getting to be a lot and just really starting to feel it in my body.'
Carries the classic rebuilder regret about trajectory rather than appearance: 'I can't imagine being more stiff and more immobile.'

Weak fit on one axis: unlike the typical rebuilder he has no prior peak to return to — he is 'new to working out' and 'been skinny all my life', so the 20s reference is about absence of pain, not lost fitness.

The defining feature of this call is not captured by any avatar in the vocabulary: high intent, high trust, zero price resistance in principle, and a genuine order-of-magnitude affordability gap ($100-500/month against $6,000). Proposed label for central clustering: 'the_priced_out_believer'.

goals.text: Put on muscle — has been skinny his whole life and knows he has to strength train to change it
Get rid of the constant stiffness in low back, shoulders and hips
Build conditioning and cardio without having to do it as a separate activity
Get back to feeling the way he did in his 20s
More energy after a 10-11 hour workday
Keep hiking and swimming on twice-yearly trips, into his 40s and 50s, without feeling broken
Be physically able to get on the ground and chase future children
Stop telling his wife his back is killing him and be better to be around
Train at home in under 45 minutes without commuting to a gym
Turn training into a consistent practice rather than something that collapses when work gets busy

pains.text: Constant low back, shoulder and hip stiffness and pain, self-rated 4-5 out of 10, present all the time and worsening over years
Pain dominates his mood and spills into his marriage — 'when you're in pain, that's all you think about'
Everything he has tried has fallen away when work gets busy — 'maybe I've done something like three times a week and then maybe that turns into twice a week and then not at all'
No idea what to do or how to progress — 'I just didn't know what I was doing. I didn't know where I was going with it'
No accountability — 'I didn't have anyone to keep me accountable'
Works 7 a.m. to 5-6 p.m. from a desk in back-to-back meetings, gets up 30-60 minutes before starting
Gym-averse — will not commute to a gym, is exhausted after work and does not know what to do there
Late-night snacking on Tim Tams and chocolate pretzels two or three times a week
Very low daily movement at 3,000-4,000 steps
Cannot afford the programme — roughly $200 a month of surplus after bills and no $6,000 available in cash or credit

objections.raw_quote: Do you? Okay. It's really high.
objections.rep_response: Challenged the framing — 'Depends on what you define as high. Depends. What do you mean with that?' — then asked whether payment was the only blocker

objections.raw_quote: I mean, it would, I just, that's way out of my price range.
objections.rep_response: Separated unwillingness from incapacity ('is it more of a, I just don't have it available at the moment, or is it more of a, yeah, I just don't want to invest it into myself?'), then ran the financial picture — available funds, monthly surplus after bills, available credit, credit score — and proposed third-party financing over 12 months

objections.raw_quote: all right i think i'm just gonna have to check it out later i i don't know yeah it's gonna be too much as in like uh too much is just overall it's just too much as even if you would be able to split it up over 12.
objections.rep_response: Backed off explicitly — 'I'm not going to force you doing it, I don't want to put you in a finance position' and 'if you say like I don't have that available I also would say like don't do it' — then set a same-day deadline to review his finances and report back

objections.raw_quote: Yeah, yeah, I'm going to look at it today after we get off this call and talk about my wife.
objections.rep_response: Accepted it without comment and moved straight to logistics for what to do if he completes payment

objections.raw_quote: so he doesn't do that at all anymore, even with, like, higher-paying clients?
objections.rep_response: Confirmed live video coaching had been discontinued — 'Overall, no. Of course, here and there, he sometimes might, but no, overall not' — and argued SMS check-ins produce better results than weekly calls

offer.payment_plan_terms: No in-house payment plan. The rep directed the prospect to third-party consumer financing, which the prospect himself named: 'is this like through Klarna or something like that?' Rep: 'Yeah, something like that. Yeah, very similar. And then you could split it up over 12 and then it will come down to round about 500 a month.' Interest was acknowledged but not quantified — 'it would have a little bit of interest with it... it depends all on what your credit score is'. The rep walked him through a live checkout link to run a credit check and told him the 'pay now' button would not take payment. No approval, no rate and no schedule were established.

evidence: No payment taken and no verbal agreement to proceed — the prospect never said yes.
A financing checkout link was sent and received ('okay i got the link'), but it was a credit-check link rather than a payment link accepted by the buyer, and he declined to complete it on the call.
Prospect deferred to review his own finances and consult his wife: 'I've got to look at my finances and see what I could do to be able to afford it' and 'talk about my wife'.
Rep set a same-day deadline: 'let me know by the end of the day what your thoughts are.'

Strong counter-evidence for treating this as lost rather than follow_up: 'that's way out of my price range', 'I don't have the money available', and 'it's just too much... even if you would be able to split it up over 12.' On the disclosed numbers — roughly $200 monthly surplus and no $6,000 in cash or credit — the deal is not affordable at any structure offered, so this is a follow_up in form and a loss in substance.

Counter-evidence the other way: intent, trust and belief were all high and unresolved by anything other than money — 'I've seen his transformation and I know he has a proven method and I think I can see myself following that.'
outcome.next_step: Prospect to review finances and speak with his wife the same day, then text or call the rep; if he completes financing, the rep schedules the Trevor onboarding meeting.

notable.note: The best-run discovery in the batch — a genuine hit on Phase 4, a strong Phase 3 that reached the marriage and future children, and the most complete money play the rep ran all week — landing on a prospect who cannot afford the programme by an order of magnitude. He disclosed roughly $200 of monthly surplus and a $100-500 ceiling against a $6,000 price, and the response was to run a live credit check for 12-month third-party financing. The rep did pull back at the end ('I don't want to put you in a finance position'), but only after walking him to a checkout page. Two secondary findings: the rep could not describe the financing product he was selling — the prospect supplied the name 'Klarna' and the rep answered 'something like that' — and the one-to-one coaching turns out to be SMS-only, with live video calls discontinued, which the prospect had to ask about four separate times to establish.

quality.notes: Repeated inversions and artefacts. The prospect's own line 'Like how it felt when I was in my 20s' is attributed to the rep at 00:00:59; the token '33' is spuriously injected into several of the prospect's turns around 00:01:32-00:01:48; the rep's question 'Do you have a pen and paper with you, Michael?' is attributed to the prospect at 00:22:32; and a long unpunctuated block from roughly 00:39:00 to 00:40:00 and again at 00:51:13 merges both speakers under one label. Roles resolved from content throughout.
